newsitem.title: USA: BASEBALL-ALOMAR DROPS APPEAL, SUSPENSION SET FOR NEXT SEASON.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-ALOMAR DROPS APPEAL, SUSPENSION SET FOR NEXT SEASON.

text.p: Baltimore Orioles second baseman Roberto Alomar decided to drop an appeal of his five-game suspension in a move aimed at ensuring that his punishment will not be enforced until the 1997 season.
The Major League Baseball Players Association informed American League officials of Alomar's decision Wednesday night.
"As far as I am concerned this matter is over," said the union's executive director Donald Fehr. "Robby reflected on it and in the last 24 hours decided to drop the appeal."
The players' union said that dropping the appeal and accepting the original suspension eliminated the need for Thursday's hearing regarding punishment for Alomar's outrageous behaviour.
American League President Gene Budig later issued a statement accepting Alomar's decision, effectively cancelling Thursday's meeting.

"The American League suspension will stand. Mr. Alomar will not play in the first five games of next season," Budig's statement said. "Mr. Alomar offered an unqualified apology to Mr. Hirschbeck and his family. It was a sincere act.
The move is sure to further anger umpires, already infuriated by what they view as an unacceptably light punishment for spitting in the face of umpire John Hirshbeck last Friday.
Budig, in his statement called the incident "a tragic event", adding, "but Major League Baseball must move forward with resolve that no such thing will ever happen again."
Alomar had appealed his five-game suspension after the incident and league officials originally set the hearing for next season.

Major League umpires delayed a threatened boycott and agreed to work playoff games Tuesday and Wednesday only after the hearing was moved up to this Thursday. Spokesmen for the umpires said Tuesday that only Alomar's immediate suspension during the playoffs would satisfy the umpires.
"There never was any possibility of a post-season suspension," claimed Fehr. "It was never discussed. It is not the established practice."
Representative for the umpires could not be immediately reached to comment on the latest development.

Major League officials had replacement umpires standing by Tuesday in case the regulars carried out their threatened boycott. It is not yet known if the umpires will protest by refusing to work Thursday's two playoff games.
Alomar has already played in the first two games of the Orioles' division series against Cleveland, going 2-for-8 with two RBI. Baltimore is next scheduled to play Friday in Cleveland.
It is possible, however, that the dispute will be back in court before that game is played.

Major League Baseball Tuesday attempted to get a judge to issue an injunction forcing the umpires to work due to a no-strike clause in their contracts. U.S. District Court Judge Edmund Ludwig instead helped both sides reach a temporary resolution to the dispute.
The umpires had argued that Alomar's actions and baseball's failure to take immediate action constitutes unsafe work conditions.

Days after saying he had no regrets over the incident, Alomar attempted to short-circuit the ugliness by issuing his apology to Hirschbeck and his family and donating $50,000 for research into the rare disease that took the life of one Hirschbeck's sons and afflicts another.
Alomar had exacerbated the situation by making comments regarding the death of Hirschbeck's son.
The late apology and donation did little to appease the umpires.
